query: For boride-based components used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment, what single intervention could improve resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment whose results could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled pre-oxidation treatment that forms a stable, adherent oxide layer on boride-based components will improve their resistance to molten aluminum corrosion.
generation.material_initial_state: Boride-based components with as-fabricated, untreated surfaces.
generation.intervention: Subject the components to a high-temperature pre-oxidation treatment (e.g., heating in air at about 900°C for 1–2 hours) to develop a continuous oxide scale.
generation.conditions: The treatment must be performed under controlled atmospheric conditions (air) and applied uniformly; effectiveness is expected under service conditions where the oxide layer remains intact (i.e., without severe mechanical disruption or exceeding its thermal stability limit).
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a coherent, adherent oxide scale—likely comprising boron oxides and minor metal oxides—that acts as a diffusion barrier.
generation.mechanism: The pre-formed oxide layer impedes direct contact between molten aluminum and the underlying boride material, reducing interfacial reactions and slowing aluminum penetration; thus, the oxidation pretreatment improves the overall corrosion resistance in the aggressive molten aluminum environment.
generation.predicted_outcome: Pre-oxidized boride components will display a significantly lower corrosion rate (e.g., reduced weight loss, less interfacial degradation) compared to untreated counterparts when exposed to molten aluminum.
generation.baseline: Boride-based components without any pre-treatment, which typically exhibit higher rates of corrosion due to direct molten aluminum attack.
generation.boundary: The benefit is expected only if the oxide scale is thermodynamically stable and mechanically adherent during exposure to molten aluminum; if service conditions lead to scale disruption or if the oxide layer degrades above certain temperatures, the corrosion resistance may not improve.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the precise composition and long-term stability of the oxide layer in prolonged exposure to molten aluminum, as well as its resistance to mechanical wear or spallation during service.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of boride-based component specimens. Apply the pre-oxidation treatment (heating in air at approximately 900°C for 1–2 hours) to one set while leaving the other set untreated. Expose both sets to molten aluminum under controlled, identical conditions. After exposure, assess corrosion via weight loss measurements, microscopic examination (SEM/EDS), and chemical analysis of the interfacial regions.
measurements: Weight loss of samples after exposure
SEM/EDS imaging of the surface and interface
Phase analysis (XRD) of the oxide scale and adjacent regions
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if the pre-oxidized samples do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in corrosion resistance (i.e., similar or higher weight loss, comparable or worse interfacial degradation) relative to the untreated control samples.
